byTheNumbers.title: The year in numbers
byTheNumbers.standfirst: The 1900 census counted a nation of about 76 million people, mostly on farms and in small towns, where a baby born that year could expect a short life by today's standard.

items.title: Population
items.summary: The 1900 census, taken on 1 June, counted the people of the United States.

sources.label: U.S. Census Bureau: 1900 Census, Volume I, Population, Part 1
Wikipedia: 1900 United States census

items.title: Life expectancy at birth
items.summary: A baby born in 1900 could expect to live about 47 years; a three-year average for 1900 to 1902 is higher, about 49.

sources.label: CDC NCHS: Life Expectancy in the U.S., 1900-2018
CDC NCHS: United States Life Tables, 2018 (National Vital Statistics Reports)

items.title: Town and country
items.summary: About two in five Americans lived in places the census counted as urban.

sources.label: Harvard CSCI E-12: United States Urban and Rural Populations (Census Bureau data)

items.metric: Share of the population living in urban places

items.title: Reading and writing
items.summary: About one person in ten could not read or write; the rate was far higher among foreign-born and Black Americans.

sources.label: Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Bc793-797: Illiteracy rate, by race and nativity, 1870-1979
Transylvania County Library: The illiteracy (cites Census Bureau, 11.3 percent)

items.title: Cars on the road
items.summary: Only a few thousand motor vehicles were registered in the whole country, all of them cars.

sources.label: FHWA Highway Statistics Summary to 1995, Table MV-200: Motor vehicle registrations
Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Df339-342: Motor vehicle registrations

items.title: People per household
items.summary: A typical household held between four and five people.

sources.label: Population Reference Bureau: average household size 1900-2010
Census chart book: Households, Relationship to Householder, and Home Ownership

foodAndKitchen.title: Food and the kitchen
foodAndKitchen.standfirst: Food took the biggest share of a working family's money, and cooking meant a wood or coal range and an icebox filled by the iceman.

items.title: Half of every dollar
items.summary: For a working-class family around the turn of the century, food was the largest item in the budget, roughly fifty cents of each dollar.

sources.label: Katherine Leonard Turner, How the Other Half Ate: A History of Working-Class Meals at the Turn of the Century (University of California Press, 2014)

items.title: A mill worker's breakfast
items.summary: Textile workers in the Southern Piedmont ate fried pork with wheat biscuits or cornbread and molasses; in Massachusetts a mill hand might have the day before's beans and bread with coffee.

sources.label: Katherine Leonard Turner, How the Other Half Ate (University of California Press, 2014)

items.title: The midday dinner on a farm
items.summary: On farms the largest meal was often at midday, and a one-pot dish could simmer while other chores were done.

sources.label: Chowhound: What the average American ate during the Industrial Revolution

dishes: a one-pot dish that simmered for hours

items.title: The icebox and the iceman
items.summary: Foods were kept cool in a wooden icebox filled with a block of ice delivered to the door.

sources.label: National Park Service: The Icebox, the Predecessor of Modern Refrigeration

items.title: Recipes with exact measures
items.summary: Fannie Farmer's 1896 Boston Cooking-School Cook Book popularised level cups and spoons, replacing a pinch or a teacup of this and that.

sources.label: Encyclopaedia Britannica: Fannie Farmer
Encyclopedia.com: Farmer, Fannie Merritt

clothingAndStyle.title: What people wore
clothingAndStyle.standfirst: Women's clothes were fitted and floor-length; many farm clothes were made at home, while men bought much of theirs ready-made.

items.title: The shirtwaist
items.summary: The tailored blouse called the shirtwaist, linked with the Gibson Girl look, could be bought ready-made for as little as 25 cents or as much as $7 in late-nineteenth-century catalogues.

sources.label: ASU FIDM Museum: 1890s Shirtwaist
Maine Memory Network: Historic clothing

items.title: The S-bend silhouette
items.summary: A corset gave day dress its S-curve shape, and skirts reached the floor.

sources.label: FamilySearch: 1900s Fashion, Clothing Styles in the Edwardian Era

items.title: Home-made on the farm
items.summary: Most farm women and children wore clothes made at home, while men bought most of theirs ready-made from store racks.

sources.label: University of Northern Colorado, Hewit Center: Clothing (Colorado farmers and ranchers)

items.title: Bib overalls
items.summary: By the early 1900s many companies made bib overalls, and catalogues and photographs show farm men as the main wearers.

sources.label: Ann Hemken, The development and use of bib overalls in the United States, 1856-1945 (Iowa State University thesis, 1993)

items.title: The sack suit
items.summary: Men's day wear centred on the sack suit, ancestor of the modern business suit, and mass production was putting ready-made clothes within reach of more people.

sources.label: FamilySearch: 1900s Fashion, Clothing Styles in the Edwardian Era

workAndWages.title: Work and wages
workAndWages.standfirst: Factory weeks ran close to sixty hours, children as young as ten were counted among the workers, and the household had its own unpaid week, starting with wash day.

items.title: A factory week
items.summary: A manufacturing wage earner worked well over fifty hours a week; estimates run from 55 to nearly 60.

sources.label: Robert Whaples, Hours of Work in U.S. History (EH.Net Encyclopedia)
Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Ba4589-4591: Average weekly hours in manufacturing, 1900-1957

items.title: Children at work
items.summary: The census recorded more than 1.75 million children aged 10 to 15 as gainfully employed, about 18 percent of that age group.

sources.label: University of Maryland, Gompers Papers: Children aged 10 to 15 engaged in gainful occupations (census data)
Carleton College Library: Census exhibit, Occupations and industry

items.metric: Children aged 10 to 15 recorded as gainfully employed

items.title: Women in paid work
items.summary: Roughly one working-age woman in five was in the paid labour force.

sources.label: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics: American labor in the 20th century

items.title: Average annual earnings
items.summary: Across all non-farm employees, a year's earnings averaged $483; across all employees, farm workers included, $418.

sources.label: Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Ba4280-4282: Daily and annual earnings of employees, 1860-1929

items.title: Monday was wash day
items.summary: Household laundry was an all-day job, usually on Monday, with ironing on Tuesday; the day could shift with the weather.

sources.label: Living History Farms: Blue Monday, wash day
University of Iowa DIY History: diary transcription, 1900

schoolAndChildhood.title: Growing up
schoolAndChildhood.standfirst: School was a term of about seven months, attended unevenly, and many children were already working.

items.title: The school year
items.summary: The average school term was about 144 days, and a pupil attended about 99 of them.

sources.label: NCES Digest of Education Statistics 2003, Table 36: school term and attendance, 1869-70 to 1999-2000
Historical Statistics of the United States, Table Bc94-96: Public school attendance and term

items.title: Compulsory school laws
items.summary: Most states had a compulsory-attendance law by 1900, though sources count between 29 and 34 and enforcement varied.

sources.label: Reason: Compulsory Schooling (1971)
History of Education Quarterly: compulsory education and child labor laws and high school attendance in New York City, 1898-1917

items.title: Toys
items.summary: Children played with rag dolls, toy soldiers, doll furniture, tea sets and simple mechanical toys.

sources.label: Rosenberg Library Museum: Toys, 1890s-1940s

schoolAndChildhood.scarcityNote: We could not verify national figures for the share of children enrolled in 1900, or for school fees and the school day. This section holds what was checked.

gettingAround.title: Getting around
gettingAround.standfirst: Cities ran on streetcars at a nickel a ride, horsecars were fading, and the fast long-distance trains came just after the year.

items.title: The nickel streetcar
items.summary: Five cents was the usual streetcar fare in cities such as Minneapolis-St. Paul and Cleveland.

sources.label: Star Tribune: A few facts about Twin Cities trolleys
Wikipedia: Streetcars in Cleveland

items.title: Electric trolley, horse and el
items.summary: In New York City in 1901 about 676 of 1,141 miles of track were electric surface trolley, 178 were elevated and 140 were still horse-drawn.

sources.label: Street Railway Journal, 5 October 1901 (LA Metro Library archive)

items.title: The end of the horsecar
items.summary: Horsecars had been a fixture of American city streets from about 1860 to 1900, before electric trolleys replaced them.

sources.label: Miami University Libraries: Horsecars, City Transit Before the Age of Electricity

items.title: The 20-hour train comes in 1902
items.summary: New York to Chicago in 20 hours was not yet available in 1900; the Pennsylvania Special and the 20th Century Limited began it in June 1902.

sources.label: American-Rails.com: Pennsylvania Railroad passenger trains
American-Rails.com: Pennsylvania Railroad's Pennsylvania Limited

items.title: Sleeping cars
items.summary: Pullman sleeping cars ran on the Pennsylvania Railroad's overnight trains under a contract dating from 1870.

sources.label: American-Rails.com: Pennsylvania Railroad passenger trains

gettingAround.scarcityNote: We found no sourced 1900 door-to-door journey times or fares, so there are no journey cards for this year.

keepingInTouch.title: Keeping in touch
keepingInTouch.standfirst: A letter cost two cents, a postcard one, and a telegram was priced by the word.

items.title: Two cents a letter
items.summary: A letter cost two cents an ounce anywhere in the United States.

sources.label: New York postal guide, 1904 (University of Wisconsin digital collections)

items.title: The one-cent postcard
items.summary: Since 1898 a postcard could travel for one cent, half the letter rate.

sources.label: U.S. House of Representatives History: Postcards

items.title: Mail to the farm gate
items.summary: Rural Free Delivery began as a trial in 1896, with $40,000 voted by Congress.

sources.label: Encyclopedia.com: Rural Free Delivery

items.title: Telegrams by the word
items.summary: A telegram was priced for a minimum of ten words, with extra words added; one example is 60 cents for ten words from New York to Georgia.

sources.label: University of Kansas Libraries: telegraph rate sources

keepingInTouch.scarcityNote: We found no sourced delivery times for letters or telegrams in 1900, so there are no message cards that can race.

healthAndMedicine.title: Health and medicine
healthAndMedicine.standfirst: Infection, not heart disease or cancer, filled the list of leading killers, and water filtration was just beginning.

items.title: What people died of
items.summary: Pneumonia and influenza, tuberculosis and diarrhoeal disease were the leading causes of death; with diphtheria they caused about a third of all deaths.

sources.label: Univ. of Illinois: 10 leading causes of death in 1900
CDC Preventing Chronic Disease: mortality analysis

sensitivity.note: This item describes deaths from disease.

items.title: Typhoid and the city water supply
items.summary: Philadelphia lost more than 5,400 people to typhoid fever in the 1890s; a filtration system built from 1900 to 1910 largely ended it.

sources.label: Encyclopedia of Greater Philadelphia: Typhoid Fever and Filtered Water
Population Reference Bureau: Clean Water's historic effect on U.S. mortality rates

sensitivity.note: This item describes deaths from disease.

items.title: Albany filters its water
items.summary: After Albany began filtering its water in 1899, typhoid deaths dropped from an average of 85 a year to 24 in the next eleven months.

sources.label: PubMed Central: Water Filtration in America

sensitivity.note: This item describes deaths from disease.

items.title: Typhoid cases
items.summary: Typhoid struck roughly 100 people in every 100,000 in 1900, against about 34 in 1920.

sources.label: CDC: History of Drinking Water Treatment

sensitivity.note: This item describes deaths from disease.

items.title: What a doctor charged
items.summary: Local records give $1 for a house call and 50 cents for an office visit; hospitals were few and most babies were born at home.

sources.label: Minnesota Academy of Medicine: The History of Medicine
OU Medical Center: 100-year history excerpt

leisureAndFun.title: Evenings, weekends and festivals
leisureAndFun.standfirst: Free time meant vaudeville, the seaside crowds of Coney Island, the bicycle and a tree in the parlour at Christmas.

items.title: A night at the vaudeville
items.summary: Vaudeville bills mixed musicians, dancers, comedians, trained animals and magicians, and had become the first modern big business in entertainment.

sources.label: New World Encyclopedia: Vaudeville
Cambridge History of American Theatre: Popular entertainment

items.title: Coney Island
items.summary: Crowds took a day trip to Coney Island's amusement parks, nine miles from Manhattan, paying a dime for sights such as a diving horse.

sources.label: Lumen Learning (William & Mary U.S. History): Leisure and Entertainment

items.title: The bicycle craze
items.summary: After safer designs arrived, bicycling became a mass pastime for both men and women.

sources.label: Lumen Learning (William & Mary U.S. History): Leisure and Entertainment

items.title: The Christmas tree
items.summary: A freshly cut tree raised in the parlour on Christmas Eve and lit with candles had become a family custom, mostly with home-made ornaments.

sources.label: Living History Farms: Gathered around the tree
Practical Preservation Services: History of the Holidays, Christmas trees

leisureAndFun.scarcityNote: We could not verify baseball attendance or Fourth of July customs for 1900, so those are left out.

spotlight.title: Gaslight to electric light
spotlight.standfirst: In 1900 most American homes were lit by kerosene lamps; electric light was a city novelty that would take until 1940 to reach nearly four in five homes.

items.title: The kerosene lamp
items.summary: The kerosene lamp was the most important modern light source in 1900 and most widely used in the United States; electricity was comparatively unimportant for home lighting.

sources.label: Business History Conference: The Global Supply of Lighting in 1900 (Leslie Hannah)

items.title: Pearl Street, 1882
items.summary: Edison's Pearl Street Station in New York began supplying 59 customers in 1882.

sources.label: U.S. Census Bureau: History and the Census, Electricity

items.title: A new trade
items.summary: The 1900 census was the first to count electricians as a separate occupation.

sources.label: U.S. Census Bureau: History and the Census, Electricity

items.title: Power for factories
items.summary: In 1900 barely 4 percent of the power used in American factories was electric, according to census statistics reported in 1903.

sources.label: Nebraska newspapers (Chronicling America): 17 January 1903

items.title: Forty years on
items.summary: The 1940 census was the first to ask about home lighting and found 78.7 percent of occupied homes had electric light.

sources.label: U.S. Census Bureau: History and the Census, Electricity
